fundEducation.summary: Understand funds — passive vs active, fees & ratings

feeCalculator.title: The impact of fees
feeCalculator.note: Red number = how much the fee costs you compared to 0.2%. Compound interest means small differences grow large over time.

passive.title: Passive (index) vs active management
passive.indexDesc: track an index, e.g. OMXS30 or MSCI World. They don't try to beat the market — they are the market. Fees are low (typically 0.1–0.4%) because no manager needs to make active decisions.
passive.activeDesc: have a manager who selects which companies to include. The goal is to beat the index. Fees are higher (typically 0.8–1.5%) to cover the manager's work.
passive.researchDesc: According to William Sharpe's arithmetic (1991), the average active fund must underperform the index by exactly the fee difference. S&P's SPIVA data confirms this: roughly 85–90% of active funds underperform their benchmark over 10 years. That doesn't mean all active funds are bad, but the odds are against you.

morningstar.title: Morningstar rating
morningstar.desc1: The rating (1–5 stars) is based on risk-adjusted historical return compared to funds in the same category. 5 stars = top 10%, 1 star = bottom 10%.
morningstar.importantDesc: The rating looks backwards, not forwards. A fund with 5 stars has performed well historically, but that doesn't guarantee future returns. The fee is often a better predictor of future performance.

tips.title: Rules of thumb
tips.tip1: Always compare the fee — it's the only thing you can control
tips.tip2: An index fund with 0.2% fee needs no manager to "beat the market"
tips.tip3: If you choose an actively managed fund — require that it has historically beaten the index after fees
tips.tip4: Spread the risks: mix geography (Sweden + Global) and asset classes (equities + bonds)
tips.tip5: Long investment horizon? More equities. Short? More bonds.
